title: I NEED HELP IN ROBLOX VIBE CODING PLEASE!
author: SyntaxFlows
selftext:
I’m trying to build a serious Roblox game while using AI agents like **Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, etc.** for as much of the development as realistically possible.

I’m basically approaching it as a **vibe coder / creative director**: I decide what the game should be, plan/review things with AI, and let agents handle a lot of the implementation through **Roblox Studio MCP**.

I’m NOT looking for “give AI one prompt and it makes the whole game.” I’m trying to understand how people who are actually good at this structure their entire workflow.

I’d love to know what your process looks like from:

**idea → game design → planning → architecture → map/environment → gameplay systems → UI → testing → polish → optimization → release**

A few things I’m especially interested in:

**AI setup:**  
Do you use one model for everything, or different models for planning, coding, 3D work, reviewing, debugging, etc.? Do you use Roblox’s MCP or a community MCP? Rojo/Script Sync? Git?

**Skills / instruction files:**  
Do you use [`SKILL.md`](http://SKILL.md), [`AGENTS.md`](http://AGENTS.md), custom rules, or your own long workflow files? How important are they? Do you keep only a few active per task, or have detailed skills for every area of development?

I’ve heard both sides: some people say too many skills just pollute context, while others have very detailed custom skills built from their own experience. I’d really like to know what works in practice.

**Maps/environment art is my biggest question.**

AI can easily make terrain, roads, trees, buildings, plazas, etc., but I keep getting results that are technically correct while still looking **generic, flat, badly composed, empty, repetitive, or obviously AI-made**.

If you’ve successfully used agents to create genuinely good-looking Roblox environments, how do you do it?

Do you:

* plan coordinates/layout first?
* use reference images or moodboards?
* generate concept art first?
* give the builder screenshots/references?
* build procedurally with Luau?
* let MCP place/edit everything directly?
* use a separate AI as an art director?
* build one finished section, screenshot it, critique it and iterate?

And which models have actually been good for **3D spatial reasoning and environment design** for you?

**Systems/programming:**  
How large of a task do you normally give an agent? One module, one complete system, or something larger?

For things like combat, inventories, shops, DataStores, vehicles, networking, etc., do you let the AI architect everything or do you design the system first and have it implement the plan?

**Testing:**  
Do you make the agent write **unit tests + integration tests**, run Roblox playtests through MCP, inspect errors and fix them before moving on?

Do you also maintain documentation/changelogs for every module/system so future agents understand what already exists?

**Knowledge required:**  
I also want opinions on this honestly. How much Lua/programming/system-design/3D knowledge do you think the human needs before this workflow actually becomes effective?

I understand the problem of not knowing enough to recognize when the AI made a bad architectural or visual decision, so I’m interested in what you personally learned versus what you delegate.

And most importantly:

**If you already built a Roblox project heavily using AI agents, what did your workflow look like at the beginning, what mistakes did you make, and what does your workflow look like NOW?**

I’m not asking anyone to reveal private/proprietary techniques. Even the general structure of a real working pipeline would be really useful.

If you have a game, video, repo, screenshots, or write-up showing what you managed to build with the workflow, I’d also love to see it.

comments.author: HawthorneTR
comments.body:
Not Roblox (my game is in Godot), but it's the same setup: I'm the creative director and Claude Code does most of the building. Here's what works for me:

**Setup:** One strong model for everything. Switching models cost more than it saved. Git from day one, committing after every finished change, because agents sometimes rewrite half a file.

**Instruction files:** I don't use long workflow docs. I keep a small folder of short memory notes, one rule each, mostly lessons learned the hard way: "test in a separate instance," "search my asset packs before generating art," "never delete visual effects to fix performance." I add one whenever I've corrected the agent on the same thing twice.

**Environments (the big one):**

* **Make the agent look at its own work.** I have small scripts that load one scene, frame the camera and save a screenshot. The agent builds, screenshots, critiques and fixes. Without that loop it's working blind and the results come out flat.
* **Finish one small area completely,** then match the rest to it.
* **Atmosphere carries the look:** fog, light shafts, particles, wet surfaces. AI skimps on these unless you insist.
* **Use real assets first.** When something has to be custom, have the agent write a script that generates it rather than placing things by hand.

**Systems:** One system per task. I decide the rules; the AI decides how to build them.

**Testing:** Small test scripts per system, plus checking tools (one scans all dialogue for broken references). The agent runs them and fixes errors before calling a task done.

**What you need to know:** You don't need to write code. You do need to read a diff, understand your engine's basics (for you: client/server, RemoteEvents, DataStores), and have strong taste, because you're the art director.

**Early mistakes:** vague asks ("build the island"), trusting "it works" without looking, letting it "optimize" by deleting effects, no git, letting the AI write the story.

**Now:** one change → agent builds, tests and screenshots it → I play it → commit → next. Slow and boring, and it works.

**For Roblox:** Studio MCP is your screenshot loop, if your setup can capture images from Studio. Set up Rojo and git early, and make one corner of your map genuinely beautiful before you lay out the rest.

comments.author: zenmatrix83
comments.body:
you mention vibe coding, but your trying more of a structure agentic develoment approarch which is different.

The most generic workflow that I find useful

1.)You and AI do research for similar projects, you want images diagrams or anything of what you want. Look for features, how they are created, get detailed explnations.

2.)That that documenation, ask the agent to create detailed planning documenation, and you review it. You can ask the ai to do adversial reviews of the planning documents till both you and it is happy. This is the biggest part that moves away from vibe coding. Vibecoding you don't care till its done, instead try and understand what is being planned and why, and try adjusting it. You don't need to know the exact code, just look at the structure

3.)At least these days Claude on its own tries to follow TDD design, at least for me , with doing red green refractoering loops

[https://www.codecademy.com/article/tdd-red-green-refactor](https://www.codecademy.com/article/tdd-red-green-refactor)

The rest is the level of input you want vs checking results later. Claude for level design and assets need alot of help, it makes very basic assets and levels, you need to give it very detailed prompts, and to be able to tell it what it needs to do better, which comes from experience. Also like the comment make sure it uses its visison capabilities to actual analyize the image, claude its self lets to use python and do scripts and check colors but not actual the image. I make it create a text description , and having it go through loops of iterations till it looks better.

The biggest thing to understand is you need to be very clear and know exactly what you want , how the llm will understand it, and where its weaknesses are ofr the best results, which just takes time

comments.author: BHTAelitepwn
comments.body: If you try to understand how people do this, maybe try to understand what you are asking instead of copy pasting AI output.
